parsed.explanation: The combined regime pairs a strongly protective state/province (public-accommodations and hate-crime law, shield law, accessible state documents, 'Most Protective' tier) with a hostile federal layer that governs every journey stage. Entry is the sharpest exposure: the Feb 2025 visa cable directs refusal where documents cast doubt on sex and invites lifetime fraud-ineligibility review; X markers are no longer processed; trans athletes are barred; and document-mismatch travellers report blocked passports and strandment. Federal facilities bans, federal custody practices (conversion-therapy-style inmate policies; documented abuse in immigration custody), and pending litigation with no shown remedy compound this. State protections operate locally but cannot cancel federal border, document, facility or custody authority. No local criminalisation of trans status.

entry_documents.exposure: Federal Feb 2025 cable: refuse cases with document discrepancy or 'reasonable doubt' on sex; consider lifetime fraud ineligibility. X markers no longer processed. Trans athletes banned. Documented blocked/confiscated passports stranding travellers; eight governments issued advisories.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports valid until expiry. Refusal requires the four-element fraud test with limited waiver and is 'never automatic'. Litigation pending; legal-aid FAQ on document rules.
entry_documents.interaction: Document discrepancy can escalate: entry refusal → fraud allegation → lifetime bar; state ID options (X on licences) do not travel across the border.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: In immigration custody, transgender men reported forced-labour programmes, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse, with guards invoking their gender identity. Federal corrections adopted conversion-therapy-style policies (hair cutting, hormone removal) from 2026 and stopped counting trans prisoners.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Not documented. Litigation exists but no shown remedy for visitors in custody.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Entry discrepancy → secondary screening → custody is the operative chain; the state's equality law does not reach federal immigration or corrections facilities.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Federal executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity nationwide, including within this state. Elsewhere states criminalise restroom use (one documented arrest, 24h in men's ward); this state has no such ban.
federal_state_facilities.protection: State public-accommodation law (in force 2008) covers gender identity in the settings a visitor uses daily; division sits in the 15-member 'Most Protective' tier with no mapped facility ban.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State protections do not pre-empt the federal facilities order in federal buildings; elsewhere-in-country arrests show the national climate following travellers between jurisdictions.

care_services.exposure: Federal orders call minors' care 'mutilation', direct investigations of schools, and propose public-insurance exclusions; subpoenas reached 20+ hospitals. These are partly enjoined.
care_services.protection: 2023 shield law protects patients and providers from out-of-state charges; state public coverage of gender-affirming care documented (2014).
care_services.interaction: Shield law directly serves visitors travelling from ban states; its narrowed post-boycott scope is unresolved, so coverage for some care categories is uncertain.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Federal counterterrorism strategy (May 2026) prioritises 'radically pro-transgender' groups; Dec 2025 reward memo uses 'radical gender ideology' language; Jan 2025 orders direct criminal investigation of 'gender ideology' in schools; DOJ subpoenaed youth medical records.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The reward criterion never lists gender ideology; the strategy states counterterrorism powers will not target mere disagreement. State equality and trans-panic-defence-repeal laws (2022) signal the opposite framing locally.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National rhetoric raises outing probability and chills reporting, but the state's enforcement apparatus is documented as protective, not threatening.

minors_guardians.exposure: Federal orders frame minors' care as criminal and direct prosecution of teachers facilitating social transition; youth-care bans in 27 states follow a visiting family; a visiting trans minor's documents fall under the same refusal/sex-doubt screening.
minors_guardians.protection: State shield law covers patients and providers; conversion therapy on minors banned since 2015; transgender-inclusive schools policy upheld through 2020.
minors_guardians.interaction: A parent travelling with a care-seeking minor gains state shield protection but remains exposed to federal document/entry rules and to the unresolved narrowing of the shield's categories.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No state-specific data on police stops, searches or airport screening of trans travellers was found. National hate-crime statistics show sexual-orientation bias at 1/7–1/5 of single-bias incidents; 2025 poll: 66% back birth-sex-only documents, 69% back sex-based athletics rules.
street_violence_police_response.protection: State hate-crime statute adds penalties for gender-identity bias; trans-panic defences abolished (2022); public-accommodation enforcement machinery exists.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: State recourse would apply to a street assault of a visitor, but charging/ prosecution statistics were not found, so enforcement in practice is unverified.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Federal passport suit, January 2025 order challenges and Oct 2025 health rules all unresolved; exposure depends on which measures are in force on the travel date. No data on enforcement of the accommodation law against venues excluding trans patrons.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Working state courts, equality commission-style enforcement, shield law, and a functioning civil society (documented suits, advocacy, national trackers) leave real local remedies.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Local remedies operate only within state authority; federal entry, document and custody decisions are contested in national courts with no shown outcome for travellers.

anchor_checks.comparison: Lower than 0.35-A: there is no universal register barring trans visitors as such — refusal is contingent on document discrepancy or sex doubt, transit is possible, and state-level daily life is protective. But the visa cable plus fraud-referral and documented strandment is a comparably severe entry exposure with weak remedy, keeping this case well above that tier.

Similar core, higher ceiling: like Kestrel Isles, the exposure is discretionary secondary screening, missed connections and administrative refusal with slow appeal. This case adds a lifetime fraud-ineligibility escalation, documented custody abuse, and a hostile national facilities regime — worse — offset by unusually strong state protections, so modestly above 0.55.

Lower than 0.75-C: Meridia's border officers are trained and respectful with a working tribunal and compensation. Here the operative federal rules affirmatively direct refusal and invite permanent bars, facilities access is federally restricted, and litigation is unresolved — no comparable documented border-side remedy exists.

parsed.synthesis: Two sovereigns interact into one regime. The state/province contributes genuinely operative protections a visitor actually uses: public-accommodations coverage, hate-crime penalties, trans-panic-defence repeal, a care shield law, and no local facility ban or criminalisation — documented, recent, and enforced through functioning courts. The federal layer governs the stages no state law reaches: visas and entry screening (discrepancy-triggered refusal plus lifetime fraud referral), passport/marker processing, government-funded single-sex facilities nationwide, and immigration or federal custody where abuse of trans detainees is documented. Because these federal exposures are universal for outed or outable travellers and their remedy is litigation not shown to work, the score sits in Elevated Risk despite the protective division: the traveller's worst plausible outcomes — stranding, entry bar, federal custody mistreatment — are federal, while everyday life inside the state is comparatively safe.
